transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-18
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Ravi Menon (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Aurora Head of AI), Tom Alvarez (Aurora DevOps), Sara Patel (Aurora CTO)

Summary:
Quick demo of Redwood's Structured Output / JSON mode and function/tool-calling capabilities. Focus on schema enforcement, guardrails for retail PII, hosted vs dedicated tradeoffs, and POC next steps for benchmarking.

Topics:
- JSON mode & schema enforcement
- Function / tool calling examples (inventory lookup, price check)
- Guardrails, validation, and reranking
- Security & compliance (SOC2, KMS, VPC)
- Performance tradeoffs: latency vs batching/quantization
- POC scoping and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood, I'll kick us off. Ravi's here to run the demo. Maya, Sara, Tom thanks for making time.
[00:12] Maya: Thanks, Lena. We had a quick agenda in the invite — mostly focused on structured output and the function calling pieces. We're evaluating for our in-store assistant and pricing tools.
[00:24] Ravi: Great, will show JSON mode, schema validation and an example where the model returns a structured product update that we then call an internal "updateInventory" function.
[00:36] Tom: Quick infra note, we care about VPC/private deployment, and we need to know if dedicated is required for compliance.
[00:45] Sara: Also curious on latency targets — we need < 150ms p50 for the in-store kiosk use-case, if possible.
[00:52] Lena: Noted. We'll show both hosted and dedicated options and what costs/latency look like.

[02:10] Ravi: Starting the Console, so here's our Structured Output toggle — JSON mode. You can upload a JSON schema here, set required fields, types, nested arrays. Example schema: productId (string), price {amount:number,currency:string}, inStock:boolean, locations: array of {storeId, qty}.
[02:40] Ravi: We enforce schema via two layers: at inference-time we ask the model to adhere to the schema and we run a verification/validator post-hoc. We can also auto-cast common mistakes, or reject and reroll depending on your policy.
[03:10] Maya: So if the model hallucinates a store ID, can we reject it server-side?
[03:16] Ravi: Yes — you can set a strict enforcement policy that rejects any output failing JSON schema validation. Alternatively set a soft policy to attempt canonicalization and call a validation function.
[03:30] Tom: What about PII and redaction? We have customer emails and phone numbers in some fields.
[03:36] Lena: We have built-in redaction configs — you can mark fields as sensitive and Redwood will mask before logs or before sending to downstream tools. For Private deployments you can configure log retention and KMS so nothing is stored unencrypted.
[04:05] Sara: Are audit logs still available if logs are masked? We need traceability for actions.
[04:12] Ravi: You can store hashed identifiers and an audit trail that shows the schema validation result, who executed the call, and which model variant served it. For enterprise we support HSM/KMS for key management.

[05:00] Ravi: Demo scenario: retail price update. I'll run a prompt that asks for a JSON response matching the schema and then simulate function calling to update inventory.
[05:20] [05:20] Ravi: Prompt: "Produce a JSON object matching the schema with updated price and locations for product 8392" — hitting the hosted endpoint first.
[05:35] [05:35] System: streaming response starts...
[05:40] [05:40] Model (stream): {\n  \"productId\": \"8392\",\n  \"price\": { \"amount\": 24.99, \"currency\": \"USD\" },\n  \"inStock\": true,\n  \"locations\": [ { \"storeId\": \"S-118\", \"qty\": 12 } ]\n}
[06:05] Ravi: The Console shows the parsed JSON and a green validation badge — passes schema. Now we'll simulate a function call: updateInventory(payload).
[06:20] Ravi: You can map output fields directly to function args in the Console — so productId -> id, locations -> locationUpdates.
[06:34] Maya: If the model returns an unexpected enum or currency we use, do you have conversion helpers? e.g., GBP -> USD.
[06:42] Ravi: We have transform hooks — pre-hooks/post-hooks — and you can add a small policy script to normalize currencies or call an external FX service via tool call before executing final update.

[07:10] Tom: On the performance side, how much does schema enforcement add to latency?
[07:15] Ravi: Minimal — the validator is lightweight. The main latency contributors are model size and batching policy. For strict live kiosks, we recommend smaller quantized models on Dedicated pools with low batch sizes and prefix caching. That gets you into the 80-150ms p50 range depending on sequence length.
[07:40] Sara: Quantized models degrade quality sometimes — for pricing we need high fidelity. What's the tradeoff?
[07:48] Ravi: Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles per workload; for numeric precision-heavy tasks like pricing, we often recommend 8-bit hybrid or BF16 pathways and per-route fallbacks to float32 for critical calls. You can tier: cheap fallback for non-critical, full-precision for confirmation steps.

[09:00] Ravi: Back to function calling — here's a tool that does a mock inventory DB call. We'll execute in the Console and show the trace: request -> model -> validated JSON -> tool call -> response. Trace includes token-level timing and costs.
[09:30] [09:30] Tool (mock): updateInventory succeeded, updated 1 store records.
[09:35] Ravi: In the Console trace you can expand the call to see validation logs, model version, kernel profile used (like cuBLAS or triton path) — we surface that for debug and perf tuning.

[10:10] Maya: For POC we need to run our dataset — 10k SKUs, 500 concurrent devices. How would you scope Dedicated versus Hosted here?
[10:20] Lena: Typical pattern: start with Hosted API for quick validation of logic, then move to Dedicated once throughput or data isolation requires it. For 500 concurrent devices at sub-200ms, Dedicated reserved pools are normal because they give predictable throughput and you can pin model variants.
[10:38] Tom: How do autoscaling and burst capacity work for Dedicated?
[10:43] Ravi: Dedicated supports configured autoscaling policies and burst capacity to a degree. You set thresholds and burst budget. However if you're SLA-sensitive, we recommend capacity commitments + a buffer. The Console shows simulated throughput curves.

[12:05] Ravi: Shifting to guardrails: we demo schema + classifier-based safety. For example, we run a quick classifier that flags if any output contains PHI or PII and then blocks the tool call.
[12:22] [12:22] Ravi: Here's a sample: model spawns a note with customerEmail field; our classifier flags it and Console shows "blocked due to PII" with remediation suggestions.
[12:36] Maya: Nice — can we auto-redact and then re-run?
[12:40] Ravi: Yes, either auto-redact and proceed, or send a request for human review via the Console. You can also wire up an approval workflow.

[14:00] Sara: A question on compliance: SOC2 plus SAML SSO for our internal users, and we'd like RBAC on routes. Do you support role-based route restrictions?
[14:10] Lena: Yes, SSO/SAML + RBAC is supported. You can create roles that limit access to specific models and routes; audit logs capture who invoked which route and what the validation result was.
[14:25] Tom: For Private deployments we want full control over KMS and key rotation.
[14:30] Ravi: Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integration; Redwood can operate with zero plaintext logs if configured. We'll share our security pack with the exact controls.

[16:05] [rough timestamp] Ravi: Quick demo of failure modes — if the model returns malformed JSON we show two options: auto-correct or reject and re-query. This is configurable per route.
[16:30] [16:30] Model (erroneous): { productId: 8392, price: USD 24.99, inStock: yes }
[16:45] Ravi: Here, Console shows parse error, and our post-processor attempted to coerce price into number but flagged currency mismatch. If strict enforcement is on, the call is rejected and we return an error object to the client.
[17:00] Maya: For our telemetry, can we get token-level cost per route?
[17:05] Lena: Yes — Console has token-level cost breakdowns and per-model dashboards. That helped other retail customers tune their batching and caching.

[18:10] Ravi: Now switching to function-calling chaining — you can have the model produce an action that triggers a sequence: validate -> lookup price history -> compute suggested price -> call update. We show a chain demo.
[18:40] [18:40] Model (stream): { action: "computeSuggestedPrice", params: { productId:"8392" } }
[18:50] [18:50] Tool: priceHistoryLookup returns 120 datapoints, avg price 26.3
[19:10] Ravi: We instrument the chain and show latencies per step. If any step fails you can configure automatic fallback to a safe price or human review.

[20:25] Tom: We run an on-prem database behind a bastion — can Redwood call internal tools safely?
[20:31] Ravi: Yes: Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC peering. For hosted, we use customer-controlled connectors (short-lived credentials) and restrict egress. There's an enterprise connector pattern we can share.

[22:00] Maya: Another concern — hallucinations that look plausible, like invented SKUs or stores. How do we catch those?
[22:08] Ravi: Strategy: schema + validators + external lookups. You can mark fields as verifiable and run a quick tool call to check existence. Turf like SKU existence is fast and we can abort if the SKU doesn't exist. We also support a rerank/verify step where we ask the model to cite a source or confidence score.

[24:00] Sara: Any notes on the latency impact of calling external validators inline?
[24:05] Ravi: It adds network hops. To mitigate, you can do asynchronous verification and optimistically proceed with low-risk updates, or use local caches/edge validators for fast checks. Redwood Optimize suggests caching TTLs based on your access patterns.

[26:10] Lena: Let's show route-based policies in the Console — here we have a route for "price-update" that has strict schema, requires RBAC role pricing-admin, and uses dedicated low-latency pool.
[26:35] [26:35] Ravi: You can also configure rollouts: canary 5% on a new quantized model with automatic fallback to previous model if latency or quality regression is detected.
[27:00] Maya: How do you detect quality regression? We have a small eval set.
[27:07] Ravi: Redwood Eval ties to prompt sets; you run periodic evals and the Console raises regression alerts tied to prompts and threshold breaches. You can block rollouts automatically.

[29:00] Tom: On pricing, curious about unit economics — what's the delta hosted vs dedicated?
[29:08] Lena: Hosted is pay-as-you-go per token; Dedicated is commit-based monthly with lower per-token costs at scale. We'll send a pricing spreadsheet with scenarios. For high throughput, Dedicated is typically cheaper per unit even after reservation.

[31:00] Ravi: Now a quick note on kernel and hardware selection — Console shows which kernel path was used (cuBLAS, triton, custom attention kernel) and we surface perf estimates. This helps debug latency spikes like noisy neighbors.
[31:20] Maya: If we get a regression in production, do you have on-call and runbooks?
[31:25] Lena: Enterprise customers get a dedicated CSM and an escalation path; we have runbooks and we can do on-call rotations depending on support tier.

[33:15] [33:15] Ravi: Demo end-to-end trace example: request identifier, validated JSON, tool calls, and final DB update, all linked in the Console with timestamps.
[33:35] Sara: That trace view will be helpful for audits.

[34:10] Maya: For the POC, what's a minimal success criteria? We want: correctness of structured output > 98% on our prompt set, latency p50 < 200ms, and secure VPC connectivity.
[34:20] Lena: That sounds reasonable. We'll scope the POC to validate those metrics.

[35:00] Ravi: One more note: function-calling is model-agnostic in Redwood — we map outputs to tool calls in the runtime so you can swap model variants and maintain the same tooling.
[35:15] Tom: Great. Anything about tokenization mismatch when we do numeric rounding?
[35:21] Ravi: We handle numeric parsing post-hoc and have helpers for rounding and canonicalization. If it's critical you can add a microservice validation step.

[36:40] [36:40] Maya: Do you have reference customers in retail we can speak to?
[36:44] Lena: Yes, we'll introduce you to a couple — I'll include references in the email.

[37:25] Sara: Ok quick recap?
[37:28] Lena: Recap: we'll send SOC2 and security pack, pricing scenarios, and the POC SOW draft. Ravi will prep POC config and perf plan. Maya will share sample prompt set and 50 example payloads. We'll slot a 2-hour scoping session on Jan 25.
[37:45] Maya: Sounds good.

[38:10] Tom: One last technical thing — can you pin a model and then change kernel/runtime without changing route?
[38:16] Ravi: You can pin model version; kernel/runtime selection is dynamic but you can pin execution profiles per route for determinism.

[39:00] [39:00] Lena: Alright, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the docs and schedule.
[39:07] Maya: Thanks all.
[39:10] Sara: Thanks.
[39:12] Tom: Bye.
